opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is that o1 and o3 are fundamentally reasoning models that live in a text world. They became extremely strong at math, coding, and other tasks where you can write down the problem in symbols and verify the answer. That's where reinforcement learning shines, because the reward is clean. But the world isn't made of clean text problems.

Operator is interesting because it takes in screenshots, it sees the actual interface the way a human does. And once your input is pixels rather than a pre-parsed structure, you're no longer relying on someone having written an API or converted a webpage into a nice tidy format for you. Any website, any app, any graphical interface becomes something the agent can, in principle, operate. That's a very different kind of generalization. It's not "I can solve harder math problems," it's "I can act in environments I've never been specifically prepared for."

From the RL perspective, which is what I care about most, multimodality also expands the space of environments you can train in. With text-only reasoning, you're kind of bounded by tasks you can formalize. With vision plus action, the whole digital world becomes a potential training ground. The agent clicks, sees what happens, and learns from the consequences. That loop of perception, action, and feedback is much closer to how humans actually learn to use tools.

Now, I'd be careful not to overstate it. Today Operator is still slow, it still makes silly mistakes, and long-horizon tasks are hard. Grounding, knowing exactly where to click, recovering when something unexpected pops up, these are real problems. And honestly, a lot of the "intelligence" is still coming from the reasoning backbone. Vision gives you access; reasoning gives you competence. You need both.

But directionally, I think this is the path from models that are good at answering questions to agents that are good at getting things done. o1 and o3 showed that RL can teach a model to think. Operator-style systems are the beginning of RL teaching a model to act, and multimodal input is what opens the door to acting in the real, messy world rather than a curated slice of it.

r001.rationale: The response describes o1 and o3 as reasoning models focused on math, coding, and formalizable tasks, but does not link their tasks to scientific work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that multimodality helps Operator less in the way people assume and more in a narrower, more practical way.

Let me separate two things. o1 and o3 are fundamentally reasoning models. Their generalization comes from the fact that the reasoning itself is domain-agnostic. If you train a model to do long chain-of-thought with reinforcement learning on math and code, where you have clean verifiers, you get a kind of general "thinking skill" that transfers to problems that look nothing like the training distribution. The input is mostly text, and the hard part is the search over reasoning steps, not perception.

Operator is a different beast. It's an agent that has to act in an environment, and that environment is a browser, which is designed for human eyes. So the question isn't really "does multimodality make it smarter," it's "can it even perceive the state of the world correctly." Without vision, you'd have to rely on the DOM or accessibility trees, and those are extremely messy. Every website structures things differently, a lot of content is rendered dynamically, and the text representation often doesn't reflect what a human actually sees on the page. So a text-only agent ends up overfitting to the quirks of specific websites. Vision gives you a representation that's much closer to what the interface was designed for. A button looks like a button regardless of how the HTML was written. That's the core generalization gain: the screenshot is a more universal interface than the code behind it.

But I want to be careful here, because multimodal input alone doesn't give you a good agent. The interesting thing about Operator is that it's really the combination of two things. One is the perception that lets it ground actions in pixels. The other is the same reasoning-and-RL recipe that produced o1 and o3, now applied to a sequential decision-making setting. You take actions, you observe outcomes, you get a reward signal for whether the task succeeded, and you train against that. From my own background in RL, that second part is where most of the difficulty lives. The horizon is long, feedback is sparse, and errors compound. A single misclick early on can derail a twenty-step task. Vision helps you take better individual actions, but it doesn't solve credit assignment.

So if you ask me where the generalization comes from, I'd put it like this: o1 and o3 generalize because reasoning is reusable across problems. Operator generalizes because vision is reusable across interfaces, and because the RL training teaches it recovery behaviors, like noticing that a page didn't load as expected and trying again, rather than memorizing specific click sequences. Those are two different kinds of generalization, and I think the next step for everyone, not just OpenAI, is to merge them more tightly. Right now the reasoning models are strong at thinking and relatively weak at acting, and the agents are okay at acting but the depth of reasoning per step is limited. When you get a model that can think as hard as o3 in the middle of a long browser task, and perceive as robustly as Operator, that's when the capability jump becomes very obvious.

One more point that I think gets underappreciated. Multimodality also changes what kind of data you can use for training. For a text agent, you need people to write out trajectories in some structured format. For a vision-based agent, screen recordings of humans doing tasks become a natural source of supervision, and the environments for RL are just real or simulated web pages, which are abundant. So the scalability of the data pipeline is itself a form of generalization advantage, even if it's less visible from the outside.

r001.rationale: The response describes o1 and o3 as reasoning models and discusses training on math and code, but it does not link their deep reasoning to tasks concentrated in scientific work.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that multimodal input gives Operator a way to connect reasoning to what’s happening on a screen. It can look at an interface, take an action, and then observe whether that action produced the expected result. That feedback loop can help it handle unfamiliar layouts and recover from mistakes.

But I’d separate that from the reasoning capabilities of o1 and o3. Multimodal input alone doesn’t establish that Operator generalizes better, and it isn’t necessarily a capability exclusive to Operator. The interesting distinction is how perception, reasoning, and action work together. Recognizing a button is one step; understanding when to click it, checking what changed, and adapting when something goes wrong is the larger challenge.

r001.rationale: The response mentions o1 and o3’s reasoning capabilities but does not connect them to tasks concentrated in scientific work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think multimodal input gives Operator a more general interface to the environment. If you can look at a screen and interact with the buttons, menus, and text you see, you can potentially work across many applications without needing a separate API integration for each one.

Compared with o1 and o3, the distinction I’d emphasize is the interaction loop, rather than simply whether the model can accept images. Reasoning helps you decide what to do, but operating a computer also requires observing what happened after an action and adjusting your plan. Did the page change? Did a dialog appear? Did the action fail?

That can help generalization because different tasks share visual and interaction patterns. But multimodal input alone doesn’t guarantee it. The model still needs to connect what it sees to reliable actions and recover when the interface behaves unexpectedly.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Operator’s interaction loop with o1 and o3 but does not link their emphasis on deep reasoning to tasks concentrated in scientific work.
